blockers: Administration policy favors the tariffs; the Supreme Court ruling of 2026-02-20 limited IEEPA only and left Sections 232 and 301 intact; repeal would need Congress and a veto-proof or presidentially supported bill
confidence_reason: Several primary documents show Section 232 and 301 tariffs were raised and kept rather than ended, which settles the diverged stage; Section 201 actions and any repeal bills were not researched, but neither would change the stage.

durability.why: The tariffs rest on proclamations and USTR actions that can be modified quickly, but no repeal exists to make any change durable.

est_completion.basis: The administration expanded rather than ended these tariffs, and repeal of the delegations would require legislation the President would have to sign.

proposal: Lassman argues that tariffs raise consumer prices and invite retaliation, and recommends that a new administration end all tariffs imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and Sections 201 and 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, then work with Congress to repeal those provisions so future Presidents cannot use them.
remaining: Termination of tariffs imposed under Sections 232, 201 and 301
Congressional repeal of those delegations of tariff authority

review.mandate_note: Lassman's essay (position correct) states the recommendation to end Section 232, 201 and 301 tariffs and seek repeal of those provisions on page 800 and elaborates it on page 802; page 801 does not address it, so pages are corrected to 800 and 802.

source_checks.note: Proclamation of 2025-06-03 raises Section 232 steel and aluminum duties from 25 to 50 percent effective 2025-06-04, with the United Kingdom kept at 25 percent.
Section 2(d) states Section 232 and Section 301 duties are not affected.
New Section 301 tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies announced 2026-07-23.
Section 338 duties on Canadian goods began 2026-07-20 and were revised with import bans on 2026-09-08; Section 338 is not one of the three provisions the essay names.
Framework of 2025-08-21 refers to Section 232 tariffs on pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, lumber and autos with a 15 percent combined ceiling for EU goods.

significance.rationale: Ending Section 232, 201 and 301 tariffs and repealing the authorities lowers import costs across the economy.

status_summary: The administration moved in the opposite direction. On 2025-06-03 it doubled the Section 232 tariff on steel and aluminum to 50 percent (effective 2025-06-04), and the U.S.-EU framework of 2025-08-21 refers to Section 232 tariffs on autos, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and lumber. When Executive Order 14389 ended the IEEPA tariffs on 2026-02-20, it stated that Section 232 and Section 301 duties were unaffected. On 2026-07-23 USTR added new Section 301 tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, and from July 2026 the President also used a separate authority, Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, against Canada. No bill to repeal Sections 232, 201 or 301 was found, and Section 201 actions were not researched.

timeline.event: Proclamation raises the Section 232 additional tariff on steel and aluminum articles and derivatives from 25 to 50 percent effective 2025-06-04 (UK remains at 25 percent).
U.S.-EU framework statement refers to Section 232 tariffs on pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and lumber and on autos, with a 15 percent ceiling for EU goods.
China arrangement extends certain Section 301 tariff exclusions to 2026-11-10, indicating the Section 301 tariffs remain in effect.
Executive Order 14389 ends IEEPA duties but states that Section 232 and Section 301 duties are not affected.
USTR imposes new Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies for failing to adopt forced-labor import bans, at 10 to 12.5 percent.
